newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Fujimori says getting tougher with Peru guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori says getting tougher with Peru guerrillas.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori said in an interview published on Friday that the longer Peru's hostage crisis dragged on, the less likely his government would cede to rebel demands.
"We are not going to give in to the terrorists' demands and, as time goes by, the offers made by the government are being progressively reduced," Fujimori told Argentina's Clarin newspaper.
"At the beginning we could have accepted some demands, but now we are convinced that we are going to accept far fewer," Fujimori said.
About 15 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas have refused to release their VIP hostages unless the Peruvian government frees 400 jailed comrades.
Holed up in the Japanese ambassador's residence since Dec. 17, the 72 captives include about two dozen Japanese businessmen, senior diplomats and Fuijimori's brother Pedro.
"I don't have the faintest idea how long it will be before there is a solution to the crisis, remember that there was a seizure in Iran that lasted 444 days," Fujimori told Clarin.
But he said he might still allow the guerrillas to leave Peru if a third country granted them asylum as part of a deal to end the siege.
"If there is a country that wants to receive them, it is one of the possibilities, although there are not many that are prepared to do so," he said.
Fujimori, who left for Canada on Friday for a crisis summit with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, said the use of force would be postponed for as long as possible.

"While possibilities for dialogue exist, we are going to do everything possible in that respect," he added, "But if a hostage were to die, for whatever cause, the situation changes and we would consider any other option."
Fujimori told another Argentine newspaper, La Nacion, his brother's plight did not influence him more than any other hostage.
"It doesn't alter anything. For me the interests of my country and national security come first," he said. "We are never again going to tolerate terrorism in Peru."
